newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine sugar glut due to speculation -govt.
newsitem.headline: Philippine sugar glut due to speculation -govt.

text.p: The Philippines' sugar glut is due to speculation by importers and not because of a tariff discount given on refined sugar imports from neighbouring firms in Southeast Asia, the Tariff Commission said in a report.

"The industry has not suffered actual injury resulting from the 35 percent margin of preference (tariff discount) granted on refined sugar under the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) preferential trading arrangements," Tariff Commission chairman Emmanuel Velasco said in the report, a copy of which was released on Monday.
The cost of locally produced refined sugar was competitive at 17.95 pesos per kg compared to imports at 26.60 pesos per kg, even at a 65 percent tariff, Velasco said.

"The surge in imports, however, is apparent in the 1994-1995 period when annual imports volume from ASEAN grew by 379 percent as compared to only 130 percent growth rate from the rest of the world," Velasco said.
This was the time when the government was conducting public hearings on its plan to put quantitative restrictions on sensitive agricultural products, he said.
The government put quantitative restrictions on "sensitive agricultural products" like sugar, rice and corn on March 3, 1996.
"Clearly, imports rose significantly between the 1995 early 1996 period due to speculations on tariff increases," Velasco said.
Philippine refined sugar imports grew from 12,155 tonnes in 1993 to 156,304 tonnes in 1996. Bulk of the the imports from 1994 to 1996 came from ASEAN countries, Velasco said.
Philippine sugar farmers and millers blamed the surge on refined sugar imports due to the 35 percent rebate given to ASEAN countries.
